transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-08
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Sara (TheraHealth Eng Mgr), Ben (TheraHealth SRE), Priya (TheraHealth CTO)

Summary:
Quick sync to review this week's benchmark results comparing Redwood setup vs baseline provider (VendorX). Discussed p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec throughput, effects of KV caching and batching, some quality checks on quantized runs, and next steps (share raw logs, run final test on customer prompts, security deep dive, pricing).

Topics:
- Benchmark numbers (hosted vs dedicated)
- Test config details (batch sizes, seq lengths, model variants)
- Latency/throughput tradeoffs and fallbacks
- Security/Private concerns and audit trail
- Next steps and pilot commercial outline

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Sara: Yep, good here.
[00:08] Ben: All good.
[00:12] Maya: Cool. Today Jonas will walk through the benchmark sheet we dropped earlier, high-level numbers then drilling into p95 tails and the config that produced them. Jonas, over to you.
[00:20] Jonas: Great thanks, so I'm screen sharing the benchmark spreadsheet, if you don't see it ping me. We ran three parallel tests: baseline provider (VendorX) using their managed endpoint, Redwood Hosted (standard, quantized q4), and Redwood Dedicated on a reserved GPU pool. Each test used the same 1k synthetic-ish prompts that mimic your mix — we also ran a 200 prompt run on your small sample you sent last week.
[00:40] Jonas: High level: p50 latency for short prompts (avg 64 tokens) - VendorX 170ms, Redwood Hosted 110ms, Redwood Dedicated 60ms. p95 tails: VendorX 490ms, Redwood Hosted 220ms, Redwood Dedicated 95ms. Throughput (tokens/sec measured at steady state) VendorX ~420 tps, Redwood Hosted ~750 tps, Dedicated ~1,450 tps.
[01:05] Sara: That's a big gap on p95, nice. Are those numbers with KV cache enabled?
[01:12] Jonas: The main runs included prefix KV cache turned on for repeated prompts; we also ran cold-start runs where there was no cache and saw p95s go up about 20-30% across providers, but Redwood still preserved a ~2x advantage on the tail.
[01:27] Ben: What's the batch size you used? Our traffic is spiky so batch sizes matter.
[01:31] Jonas: Right — for these tests we used an adaptive batching config: target batch 8, max 32, time-slo 50ms. For the Dedicated runs we could push the batcher more aggressively (target 12, max 64) without impacting p95 because of the larger GPU memory and kernel fusion optimizations.
[01:48] Priya: Wait, kernel fusion optimizations — can you explain briefly what that buys us?
[01:52] Jonas: Sure, so Redwood's runtime selects kernels based on op shapes and sequence length distribution; on our Dedicated hardware we can use fused attention kernels and lower-precision paths which lower per-token compute and memory movement — that drops both latency and throughput variance. In short, fewer context switches on the GPU and better utilization.
[02:12] Sara: Any quality change with the quantized runs? We care about hallucination/regression.
[02:16] Jonas: Good question — we ran an eval set of 500 prompts comparing logits/answers. At q4 we saw micro-deltas on a handful of QA prompts, roughly a 1.2% drop in exact match vs FP16 baseline, but most semantic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-ish proxies) were within noise. We flagged the prompts where model deviated and included those examples in the sheet.
[02:40] Ben: So if we can't accept that 1% on some prompts what's the path?
[02:44] Jonas: We can do hybrid configs: keep sensitive routes on FP16 (or unquantized) and use q4 for bulk traffic. Also Redwood supports targeted per-route quantization in the routing layer so you can pin high-sensitivity prompts to higher-precision variants.
[02:58] Maya: And fallback policies — if quantized returns low confidence or the eval triggers, we can auto-fallback to FP16 for that request.
[03:06] Sara: Nice. On the throughput numbers, are you including network egress + ingress times or just service processing?
[03:11] Jonas: These are end-to-end from client's SDK call to response completion inside our test harness with a 5ms synthetic network latency injected to mimic cross-AZ hops. VendorX had higher network wait in our setup because their endpoint throttled more aggressively during bursts.
[03:25] Priya: Do you have token accounting breakdown? Cost estimates are important for us.
[03:30] Jonas: Yep that's in the sheet — tokens generated vs input, and rough compute seconds. We'll convert that into a pilot pricing sheet (Maya will lead on that) for a 3-month Dedicated pilot scenario.
[03:40] Ben: One red flag for us is p95 variance under cold cache; since our workload has many unique prompts that might blow up tails.
[03:46] Jonas: Totally: for high-uniqueness workloads, we'll recommend smaller batch windows (lower time-slo) and more aggressive prefix caching where possible. For Dedicated you also get larger KV capacity which helps repeated sub-sequences. We can also pre-warm common prefixes if you can share the top 200 prompts — that was in the next steps.
[04:05] Sara: We can do that. We'll prepare the 200 prompts and mark which are high-sensitivity.
[04:10] Maya: On security / Private options — Lena, want to remind them what we shared?
[04:14] Lena: Sure. We already shared SOC2 A3 (redacted) and an overview of our Private VPC architecture. For Private we do customer-managed VPC peering, KMS integration for key lifecycle, plus audit logs with daily retention options. We can also run the Dedicated pilot inside their VPC if you want a stronger isolation guarantee.
[04:32] Priya: For regulated data we need HSM-backed keys and at-rest encryption verification. Is that supported out-of-box?
[04:38] Lena: We integrate with customer KMS and can support HSM via your KMS provider. We'll scope the deep-dive with your security team to confirm attestation and logging details.
[04:48] Sara: Anything in the benchmarks about error rates or retry behavior? We saw some 5xxs in VendorX during one of the burst windows.
[04:55] Jonas: Yes — VendorX had a 2.1% error spike during simulated burst. Redwood Hosted had 0.3% and Dedicated ~0.04% (mostly transient network). We included the raw logs in the artifact link. Error modes were rate-limit responses and occasional out-of-memory retries on VendorX.
[05:15] Ben: That OOM is worrying. Is that because they shard differently?
[05:18] Jonas: They do a per-request instance allocation which isn't as memory-efficient; Redwood's runtime shares KV caches and reuses a warm pool, reducing OOM surface.
[05:28] Sara: Ok that's helpful. Thoughts on running a final 200-prompt run on our actual traffic? Should we do Hosted or Dedicated?
[05:34] Maya: For the final run we recommend Hosted first (lower friction), and then run Dedicated to show delta after you confirm configuration. If results look good we propose starting the Dedicated pilot.
[05:43] Priya: What's the timeline for that? We want to make a decision by end of month.
[05:46] Maya: If you share prompts by 9/14 we can run and return results in two business days, and the security deep-dive would be the week after. That keeps you on track to decide by end of month.
[05:58] Jonas: One more note on fairness of the comparison — we matched model checkpoints as closely as possible but VendorX is running a slightly newer opt checkpoint which had a higher baseline quality metric; we called that out in the sheet so you can see quality-vs-latency tradeoff.
[06:12] Sara: Good call. Anything else on config reproducibility? We need exact seed/torch/oversion etc so our infra team can validate.
[06:18] Jonas: We included an infra tab showing runtime versions, kernel flags, GPU type (A100-80GB for Dedicated runs in our lab), driver versions, container image tags and the exact CLI commands we used.
[06:30] Ben: For Dedicated pilot what does scaling look like — can you handle our peak hourly load of ~20k requests/min?
[06:36] Jonas: With Dedicated and burst pool enabled, yes — we can reserve a base pool to handle sustained load and allow burst nodes to spin up to handle peaks; we'll size the pool in the pilot commercial outline. For the 20k req/min we estimated needing roughly 6 reserved GPUs plus burst to 10, but we'll finalize after we run the customer prompt set.
[06:56] Priya: Can SLA include p95 target?
[06:59] Maya: Yes, pilot SLA can include p95 targets and we can instrument SLO alerts. We'll include escalation paths in the commercial doc.
[07:07] Sara: One admin question — how do team roles map? Who do we contact for ops issues?
[07:11] Lena: CSM for ops coordination (Lena), SE for technical (Jonas), AE for commercial (Maya). We'll add an on-call rotation if you want production support in pilot.
[07:21] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps. We'll share the raw benchmark CSVs and logs (Jonas) by 9/10, Maya will send pilot pricing and commercial outline by 9/12, Lena will schedule a security deep-dive with Priya and team by 9/11, and Sara will send the 200 prompts by 9/14.
[07:41] Priya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:43] Sara: Thanks.
[07:45] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links and invites.
[07:50] (call ends)
